```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("../../../R/00_config.R")
source("../../../R/01_bsr_core.R")
library(EmpiricalCalibration)

bsr_res <- readRDS(file.path(OUT_DIR, "data", "bsr_results_v34.rds"))
sim     <- readRDS(file.path(SIM_DIR, "simulation_merged_v34.rds"))
ci_sim  <- readRDS(file.path(SIM_DIR, "ci_simulation_merged.rds"))
nc      <- readRDS(file.path(DATA_DIR, "negative_controls_expanded.rds"))
bb      <- bsr_res$bb
gdmt    <- bsr_res$gdmt

bb_bf <- bb$boot$bf_median
bb_lo <- bb$boot$bf_ci_lo
bb_hi <- bb$boot$bf_ci_hi
gdmt_bf <- gdmt$boot$bf_median
sl_bf <- bsr_res$sl$bf
sl_lo <- bsr_res$sl$bf_ci_lo
sl_hi <- bsr_res$sl$bf_ci_hi

ci_reps <- ci_sim$reps
ci_conds <- ci_sim$conditions
ci_decisive <- !is.na(ci_reps$ci_class) & ci_reps$ci_class != "competitive"
ci_decisive_rate <- 100 * mean(ci_decisive)
ci_decisive_acc <- 100 * mean(ci_reps$ci_class[ci_decisive] == ci_reps$true_class[ci_decisive])
```

# eAppendix 1. Detailed Methods

## Notation and setting

Consider an observational study estimating the effect of a binary treatment $A$ on an outcome $Y$. The target causal estimand is the average treatment effect on the log relative risk scale, $\psi = \log \text{RR}_{\text{true}}$. After applying an estimator $\hat{\psi}$ (eg, TMLE with SuperLearner-based nuisance function estimation), we obtain a point estimate $\hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}}$ with estimated standard error $\hat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}$.

In addition to the primary outcome $Y$, the investigator has $K$ negative control outcomes $N_1, \ldots, N_K$. Each negative control $N_k$ shares the confounding structure of $Y$, meaning the same set of unmeasured confounders affects both $N_k$ and $Y$, but $N_k$ is not causally affected by treatment $A$. For each control, the same estimator $\hat{\psi}$ is applied to obtain $\hat{\gamma}_k$, the estimated log relative risk associating $A$ with $N_k$, along with its standard error $\hat{\tau}_k$.

The key working assumption is **shared bias structure** (also termed bias exchangeability): conditional on measured covariates, the distribution of residual bias affecting the primary estimate $\hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}}$ is approximately the same as the distribution governing the negative control estimates $\hat{\gamma}_1, \ldots, \hat{\gamma}_K$. We use the term bias exchangeability to distinguish this assumption from the standard causal exchangeability assumption (no unmeasured confounding); the two are related but distinct. Under bias exchangeability, the negative controls form a sample from the bias-generating process, allowing empirical estimation of the bias distribution. This assumption, like the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption it is meant to diagnose, cannot be directly verified from the data; its plausibility must be assessed through domain knowledge and sensitivity analyses.

## Definition of the credibility metric

Let $\mu_B$ denote the mean systematic bias. Under the bias exchangeability assumption, $\mu_B$ can be estimated from the negative controls: $\hat{\mu}_B$ is obtained by fitting an empirical null distribution to $\{(\hat{\gamma}_k, \hat{\tau}_k)\}_{k=1}^K$ [@schuemie2014interpreting]. The bias-corrected (calibrated) estimate is $\tilde{\psi} = \hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}} - \hat{\mu}_B$, with calibrated standard error $\tilde{\sigma} = \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}^2 + \hat{\sigma}_B^2}$, where $\hat{\sigma}_B$ is the estimated between-control heterogeneity in bias.

$$\mathrm{BF} = \frac{|\hat{\mu}_B|}{|\hat{\mu}_B| + |\tilde{\psi}|} = \frac{|\hat{\mu}_B|}{|\hat{\mu}_B| + |\hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}} - \hat{\mu}_B|}$$

BF is the share of the total calibrated signal, bias plus residual effect, attributable to systematic bias. It lies in [0,1] by construction; BF = 1 when the calibrated estimate is exactly zero, and BF = 0 when no systematic bias is estimated. The value 0.5 marks equal contributions of bias and residual effect; 1/3 marks a residual effect twice the bias.

**Rationale for the bounded form.** The ratio form is preferred over a bias difference ($|\hat{\mu}_B| - |\tilde{\psi}|$) because, on the log relative risk scale, it is scale-invariant and directly captures the question of interest: of the signal that survives calibration, how much is bias? The specific choice of denominator, total calibrated signal rather than the residual effect alone, makes the metric bounded. The unbounded bias-effect ratio, $\mathrm{BER} = |\hat{\mu}_B| / |\tilde{\psi}|$, carries the same information through $\mathrm{BF} = \mathrm{BER}/(1+\mathrm{BER})$; the bounded scale avoids the ratio's instability when the denominator approaches zero and removes the need for special handling of infinite values at the null. We report BER as an auxiliary display.

**Observed bias fraction.** A companion quantity, the observed bias fraction (OBF), divides the estimated bias by the uncalibrated estimate: $\mathrm{OBF} = |\hat{\mu}_B| / |\hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}}|$. OBF answers "of the association as estimated before calibration, what share is bias?" In the beta-blocker analysis OBF = `r round(abs(bb$bsr$mu_bias) / abs(bb$bsr$log_rr_uncal), 2)`: the estimated bias is comparable to the entire observed association. In the GDMT analysis OBF = `r round(abs(gdmt$bsr$mu_bias) / abs(gdmt$bsr$log_rr_uncal), 2)`. OBF is descriptive and unbounded; all classifications use BF.

The metric is computed directly from quantities already produced by the OHDSI empirical calibration pipeline [@schuemie2014interpreting; @schuemie2018empirical] using the EmpiricalCalibration R package, and therefore requires no additional data beyond the negative control estimates and the primary estimate.

## Confidence interval for BF

A 95% confidence interval for BF is constructed through nonparametric bootstrap with $B = 2000$ resamples, as follows. For each iteration $b = 1, \ldots, B$: (1) resample the $K$ negative control estimates $\{(\hat{\gamma}_k, \hat{\tau}_k)\}$ with replacement; (2) refit the empirical null distribution to obtain $\hat{\mu}_B^{(b)}$ and $\hat{\sigma}_B^{(b)}$; (3) compute the bias-corrected estimate $\tilde{\psi}^{(b)} = \hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}} - \hat{\mu}_B^{(b)}$, holding the primary estimate $\hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}}$ fixed; (4) compute $\mathrm{BF}^{(b)} = |\hat{\mu}_B^{(b)}| / (|\hat{\mu}_B^{(b)}| + |\tilde{\psi}^{(b)}|)$. The 95% CI is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of $\{\mathrm{BF}^{(b)}\}$ on the logit scale, back-transformed to [0,1]; equivalently, it is the percentile CI of BER on the log scale, transformed to BF. The point estimate is the bootstrap median on the logit scale, back-transformed, so the point estimate and the CI come from the same distribution. The bootstrap resamples only the negative controls because the dominant source of uncertainty for BF is the estimation of $\mu_B$ from a finite set of negative controls. As an alternative, Fieller's theorem provides a closed-form confidence set for the underlying ratio that may offer better coverage when the denominator is near zero [@fieller1954interval].

## Fieller confidence sets

The signed ratio $\rho = \mu_B / \tilde{\psi}$ underlies BF through $\mathrm{BF} = |\rho|/(1+|\rho|)$. With $m_1 = \hat{\mu}_B$, $m_2 = \tilde{\psi}$, $v_{11} = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\mu}_B)$, $v_{22} = \hat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}^2 + v_{11}$, and $v_{12} = -v_{11}$ (the primary estimate is independent of the negative controls), the Fieller set at level $1-\alpha$ contains all $\rho$ satisfying $(m_1 - \rho m_2)^2 \le z^2_{\alpha/2} (v_{11} - 2\rho v_{12} + \rho^2 v_{22})$ [@fieller1954interval]. We estimated $v_{11}$ from the variance of $\hat{\mu}_B$ across bootstrap resamples.

For the beta-blocker analysis the set was exterior, $(-\infty, `r round(bb$fieller$lo, 2)`] \cup [`r round(bb$fieller$hi, 2)`, \infty)$: only ratios inside [`r round(bb$fieller$lo, 2)`, `r round(bb$fieller$hi, 2)`] are excluded at 95%. The calibrated estimate ($\tilde{\psi} = `r round(bb$bsr$log_rr_true, 3)`$) is tiny relative to its uncertainty, so the ratio is poorly identified in the frequentist sense; the bootstrap CI on BF nevertheless lies entirely above 0.5, and the zone assignment is unaffected. For GDMT the set was interior, [`r round(gdmt$fieller$lo, 2)`, `r round(gdmt$fieller$hi, 2)`], straddling 1, consistent with the mixed classification. When the calibrated estimate is near zero, no interval method can pin down the ratio; readers should rely on the zone assignment from the BF bootstrap CI and on the calibrated p-value.

## Relationship to existing approaches

The proposed metric extends empirical calibration [@schuemie2014interpreting; @schuemie2018empirical] by providing a continuous credibility measure alongside the binary calibrated p-value. The calibrated p-value answers "Is there evidence of an effect after accounting for bias?" while the metric answers "What share of the surviving signal is bias, and does enough of an effect remain to be meaningful?"

The E-value [@vanderweele2017evalue] quantifies the minimum strength of unmeasured confounding required to explain away an observed association, a hypothetical sensitivity analysis. The proposed metric, in contrast, is empirically grounded in observed negative control data. The two approaches are complementary: the E-value asks what *would* need to be true, while the calibration-based metric estimates what the negative controls *actually indicate* about the bias present in the data.

## Estimation procedure

**Step 1: Empirical null estimation.** Fit the model $\hat{\gamma}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_B, \sqrt{\hat{\tau}_k^2 + \sigma_B^2})$, $k = 1, \ldots, K$, using maximum likelihood as implemented in the `fitNull` function of the EmpiricalCalibration R package [@schuemie2014interpreting]. This produces $\hat{\mu}_B$ and $\hat{\sigma}_B$.

**Step 2: Bias-corrected estimate.** Compute $\tilde{\psi} = \hat{\psi}_{\text{obs}} - \hat{\mu}_B$ with calibrated standard error $\tilde{\sigma} = \sqrt{\hat{\sigma}_{\text{obs}}^2 + \hat{\sigma}_B^2}$.

**Step 3: Credibility metric calculation.** Compute $\mathrm{BF} = |\hat{\mu}_B| / (|\hat{\mu}_B| + |\tilde{\psi}|)$. Obtain a 95% confidence interval using the logit-scale nonparametric bootstrap ($B = 2000$).

**Consistency property.** Under the bias exchangeability assumption and standard regularity conditions, $\hat{\mu}_B$ is consistent for $\mu_B$ as $K \to \infty$, and $\tilde{\psi}$ converges in probability to $\psi$. The map $f(\mu_B, \psi) = |\mu_B|/(|\mu_B| + |\psi|)$ is continuous at every point of the parameter space, including $\psi = 0$, where $f(\mu_B, 0) = 1$. By the continuous mapping theorem, BF is consistent for the population bias fraction over the whole parameter space, with no exclusion of the null. This contrasts with the unbounded ratio, whose population limit diverges at the null. The denominator of BF is $\tilde{\psi}$, not the true effect $\psi$; the metric does not estimate the true treatment effect.

## Threshold asymmetry

The thresholds 1/3 and 0.5 are asymmetric on the logit scale. A symmetric alternative would use 1/3 and 2/3. We adopt the asymmetric design deliberately: in observational research, the cost of a false causal claim exceeds the cost of excessive caution. This conservative asymmetry biases classification toward the bias-dominated zone, which we view as appropriate given the stakes of causal claims from observational data. BF = 1 (calibrated estimate exactly zero) is classified as bias-dominated.

## Negative control overlap and cautions

Some negative controls share overlapping outcome definitions: the "infection" category encompasses urinary tract infection and cellulitis as subcategories. This nesting means the 12 controls do not represent 12 fully independent observations, which could lead to underestimation of $\hat{\sigma}_B$ and overly narrow bootstrap CIs. The leave-one-out sensitivity analysis provides a partial check: removing any single control, including the nested ones, did not change the qualitative classification. The "fall" outcome warrants caution, as beta-blockers may increase fall risk through bradycardia or orthostatic hypotension, potentially violating the no-causal-effect assumption. However, the observed protective association for falls (RR < 1) is opposite in direction to the expected adverse effect. Confounding thus appears to dominate any causal effect; the leave-one-out analysis confirmed that excluding "fall" did not alter the bias-dominated classification.

# eAppendix 2. What BF Does Not Estimate

The metric **does not** estimate the true treatment effect; it summarizes the relationship between estimated bias and the residual effect after calibration. A bias-dominated classification means "the calibrated estimate does not support a causal claim," not "the true effect is zero." The metric also **does not** identify the source of bias, whether healthy-adherer confounding, indication bias, or other sources of unmeasured confounding. The metric **does not** provide a probability or posterior distribution over the true effect. When $\tilde{\psi} \approx 0$, a BF near 1 could reflect either a genuinely null treatment effect or a bias that approximately cancels a non-zero true effect. The metric cannot distinguish these cases.

# eAppendix 3. When Calibration-Based Diagnostics Should Not Be Used

**Insufficient negative controls.** With $K < 5$, the empirical null estimate is too imprecise. We recommend at least 8-10 controls with adequate event counts.

**Non-exchangeable controls.** If negative controls are affected by outcome-specific mechanisms that do not operate on the primary endpoint, the bias distribution will be misleading.

**Heterogeneous bias directions.** The empirical null model assumes negative controls are affected by bias in the same direction. If controls show bias in opposite directions, $\hat{\mu}_B$ will be attenuated toward zero, producing an overly optimistic BF.

**Small residual effects.** When the true treatment effect is near zero, the denominator of the underlying ratio is near zero. On the BF scale this appears as values near 1, wide bootstrap CIs, and unbounded Fieller sets. This correctly signals that the calibrated estimate is uninformative; read BF near 1 as signal saturation by bias, not as a precise fraction.

# eTable 1. Comparison of BF and Calibrated p-Value

| Feature | BF | Calibrated p-value |
|---------|-----|-------------------|
| Output type | Continuous fraction in [0,1] | Binary significance test |
| Question answered | How large is bias relative to residual effect? | Is there evidence of an effect after bias correction? |
| Scale | Scale-invariant, bounded | Depends on sample size |
| Interpretation when non-significant | Distinguishes "bias dominated" from "borderline" | Cannot distinguish these scenarios |
| Behavior at the null | BF = 1 | p close to 1 |
| Computation | From OHDSI pipeline quantities | From OHDSI pipeline |
| Recommended use | Alongside calibrated p-value and CI | Current standard |

# eTable 2. Simulation Study Design

```{r etable2-sim-design}
sim_design <- data.frame(
  Factor = c("True effect size (psi)", "Systematic bias (mu_B)", "Bias heterogeneity (sigma_B)",
             "Number of negative controls (K)", "Exchangeability violation"),
  Levels = c("0, -0.05, -0.10, -0.15, -0.20, -0.30, -0.40 (7)",
             "-0.05, -0.10, -0.15, -0.20, -0.30, -0.40 (6)",
             "0.05, 0.10 (2)",
             "12, 25 (2)",
             "0%, 30% (2)"),
  Count = c("7", "6", "2", "2", "2")
)
knitr::kable(sim_design,
  col.names = c("Factor", "Levels (count)", "N levels"),
  caption = "Simulation study design. Total: 7 x 6 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 336 conditions, 200 repetitions each (67,200 total). BF_true values span {0.111, 0.143, 0.200, 0.250, 0.273, 0.333, 0.400, 0.429, 0.500, 0.571, 0.600, 0.667, 0.727, 0.750, 0.800, 0.857, 0.889} plus the null (BF_true = 1). The 30% violation level is implemented as round(K x 0.3) shifted controls, 4/12 = 33.3% for K = 12 and 8/25 = 32.0% for K = 25.")
```

# eTable 3. CI-Based Classification Heuristic Results

```{r etable3-ci-sim}
ci_summary <- data.frame(
  Zone = c("Bias-dominated (BF_true > 0.5 or null)",
           "Mixed (1/3 <= BF_true <= 0.5)",
           "Effect-dominated (BF_true < 1/3)",
           "Overall"),
  N_reps = c(sum(ci_reps$true_class == "bias-dominated"),
             sum(ci_reps$true_class == "competitive"),
             sum(ci_reps$true_class == "effect-dominated"),
             nrow(ci_reps)),
  Point_Acc = c(
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "bias-dominated", ], mean(pt_class == true_class)),
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "competitive", ], mean(pt_class == true_class)),
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "effect-dominated", ], mean(pt_class == true_class)),
    100 * mean(ci_reps$pt_class == ci_reps$true_class)),
  CI_Acc = c(
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "bias-dominated", ], mean(ci_class == true_class, na.rm = TRUE)),
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "competitive", ], mean(ci_class == true_class, na.rm = TRUE)),
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "effect-dominated", ], mean(ci_class == true_class, na.rm = TRUE)),
    100 * mean(ci_reps$ci_class == ci_reps$true_class, na.rm = TRUE)),
  CI_as_Competitive = c(
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "bias-dominated", ], mean(ci_class == "competitive", na.rm = TRUE)),
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "competitive", ], mean(ci_class == "competitive", na.rm = TRUE)),
    100 * with(ci_reps[ci_reps$true_class == "effect-dominated", ], mean(ci_class == "competitive", na.rm = TRUE)),
    100 * mean(ci_reps$ci_class == "competitive", na.rm = TRUE))
)
knitr::kable(ci_summary, digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Zone", "N repetitions", "Point-estimate accuracy, %",
                "CI-based accuracy, %", "CI classified as mixed, %"),
  caption = sprintf("CI-based classification heuristic vs point-estimate rule across all 336 conditions (67,200 repetitions). The CI-based rule issued a decisive (non-mixed) classification in %.1f%% of repetitions; those decisive calls were %.1f%% accurate.", ci_decisive_rate, ci_decisive_acc))
```

# eTable 4. Leave-One-Out Sensitivity Analysis

```{r etable4-loo}
loo_tab <- data.frame(
  Excluded = bsr_res$loo$excluded_nc,
  BF = round(bsr_res$loo$bf, 3),
  Zone = ifelse(bsr_res$loo$bf > 0.5, "Bias-dominated",
         ifelse(bsr_res$loo$bf < 1/3, "Effect-dominated", "Mixed"))
)
knitr::kable(loo_tab,
  col.names = c("Excluded negative control", "BF", "Zone"),
  caption = sprintf("Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Full-data BF = %.2f. All %d exclusions remained in the bias-dominated zone (BF > 0.5).", bb_bf, nrow(loo_tab)))
```

```{r etable8-target-protocol}
    "Operationalized by the maximum prescribed beta-blocker dose as a percentage of the guideline-recommended target dose during the index hospitalization, dichotomized at 50%.",
    "No randomization; treatment classification based on achieved dose at time zero (end of 7-day grace period). Baseline confounding addressed by TMLE adjustment for 10 covariates and by negative control calibration.",
    "Operationalized as the interval days 8 to 365 from admission, with all-cause death ascertained from MIMIC-IV date-of-death records (in-hospital and post-discharge) and survivors administratively censored at 1 year.",
    "Same endpoint, captured as a binary indicator of death within the follow-up window.",
    "Same intention-to-treat-like contrast for a point-treatment strategy classified at time zero; not a per-protocol analysis.",
    "Baseline exchangeability conditional on 10 baseline covariates is plausible; bias exchangeability (shared bias structure) is addressed by negative control calibration [@schuemie2014interpreting].",
    "TMLE with SuperLearner (SL.glm sole learner) for both nuisance models, MICE imputation with 5 datasets, empirical null fitting via EmpiricalCalibration, BF with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (B = 2000), prespecified sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out negative control, SuperLearner library variation, grace period 3-14 days, GDMT known-effect comparison)."),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(target_protocol, longtable = TRUE,
  col.names = c("Protocol component", "Target trial", "Observational emulation"),
  caption = "Specification of the target trial protocol and its observational emulation, following TARGET template 1. The hypothetical trial and the observational emulation share the same causal estimand; the observational emulation uses an achieved-dose point treatment and adjusts for unmeasured confounding through negative control calibration. eFigure 7 documents the participant flow.")
```

Continuous variables are reported as mean (SD); skewed variables (creatinine, troponin T, NT-proBNP) are reported as median [interquartile range]. Categorical variables are reported as n (%). Standardized mean differences (SMDs) compare the two treatment strategies; values below 0.1 indicate adequate balance. Laboratory values with substantial missingness (potassium 72.1%, sodium 95.9%, troponin T 58.9%, NT-proBNP 84.4%, creatinine and eGFR 3.3%, hemoglobin 5.4%) were imputed by multiple imputation by chained equations with 5 datasets for the primary TMLE analysis.")

# eAppendix 4. RECORD-PE Reporting Checklist

The study is reported following the RECORD-PE (REporting of studies Conducted using Observational Routinely-collected health Data for Pharmacoepidemiology) guidelines [@langan2018recordpe]. The completed checklist is available from the authors upon request.

# eAppendix 5. TARGET Trial Emulation Checklist

The target trial emulation is reported following the TARGET (Transparent Reporting of Observational Studies Emulating a Target Trial) statement, published simultaneously in JAMA and BMJ in 2025 [@cashin2025target]. The TARGET guideline organizes 21 reporting items into six sections (abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, other information) and is supplemented by template 1 for the target trial protocol and its observational emulation and by a flow diagram template for emulations with a unique time of eligibility and treatment strategies distinguishable at baseline. The completed 21-item checklist is provided in eTable 7, the target trial protocol and observational emulation in eTable 8, baseline characteristics by treatment strategy in eTable 9, and the participant flow diagram in eFigure 7. The emulation was not prospectively registered because it is a methodological illustration.
